# Trolls in Several Forms

*Pages PDF 84-93*

## ## Trolls in Several Forms
## **Monsters in the Wilds**
Foul-tempered and evil-smelling, Trolls are among the most dangerous threats one might wish to avoid. Countless subspecies exist, all perfectly adapted to their environment. In barren mountain passes, Dwarf Rangers watch the slopes for any sign of Stone Troll activity. Sailors keep a careful eye on patches of river muck that might conceal lurking River Trolls. And in the rural wilds of the Empire, every peasant should know to take care when investigating an abandoned hovel, for fear the Common Troll who emptied it still lairs inside. 

Stranger Trolls haunt the north lands, mutated monsters more horrifying than even their own base kin. Only those with a death wish would willingly seek out a Troll. 

Trolls can be found throughout the world. There are many different subspecies, but they share similar traits. They are all monstrously strong and can regenerate any wound, save those caused by fire. When stressed, Trolls may retch up the contents of their stomach, sending a spray of bile upon their foes that can melt through armour and eat away flesh and bone. They are driven by hunger, eating anything they find, even rocks. And they are phenomenally stupid. 

Orcs and Goblins seek to lure Trolls into accompanying their tribes when they make war. However, only creatures as heedless of collateral damage as Orcs and Goblins would risk making an alliance with such beasts. 

## **Types of Troll**
Trolls adapt to their habitat, exhibiting great variation in form. Even those grouped under the banner of a particular type can exhibit a great deal of diversity in shape, colouration, and habits. With that said, most scholars of the Old World identify the following varieties. 

## **Chaos Trolls**
Chaos Trolls, sometimes known as Dark Trolls, are those who bear clear signs of having been warped by the corrupting touch of the Ruinous Powers. They tend to be larger than other trolls, and whilst their skins can be of various hues, they are often black, or shades of grey and deep blue. 

## **Common Trolls**
There is some disagreement over what a Common Troll is. There are scholars who suggest that there is a form of Troll that is found throughout several different environments that conforms to a general appearance, having dark green or grey skin, thick scales upon its scalp and back, ragged and pendulous ears, and a broad, flat nose. 

Others disagree and cite all manner of Trollish types that are simply bundled together in the category of Common Troll because they do not exhibit the particular features that would identify them as another type. 

## **Stone Trolls**
Stone Trolls live underground or in mountainous regions. They have rock-hard skin and are naturally resistant to magic. Many Stone Trolls wander the slopes and passes of the Worlds Edge Mountains, where they often fall in with the tribes of Orcs or Night Goblins that are prevalent there. Stone Trolls tend to be taller and skinnier than other forms of Troll, with long arms that reach down to the ground. 

Their scales are more apparent and develop into craggy, horny thick growths. Their hides are often grey or greyblue, and their facial features are often rather outsized, with long, bulbous noses, thick lips, and beady yellow eyes. 

## **River Trolls**
River Trolls live in bogs and along untamed riverbanks. They partially submerge themselves in swamps or brackish ponds to sneak up on and ambush their prey. River Trolls are slimy creatures that reek of rotten fish. In comparison to other Trolls, they are squat and dumpy, with bloated bellies. They sometimes share features in common with the aquatic beasts that form the great part of their diet, with small, overlapping scales, green flesh, webbed hands and feet, and hanks of hair like dripping river weeds. 

Chaos Trolls often manifest mutations, growing horns and spines from their heads, backs, and shoulders, or developing an extra head. The regenerative abilites of Trolls only seems to exacerbate their mutated appearance. Rather than simply closing over, the raw flesh of a wound will form into a new mouth or sprout fronds of slender tentacles. They are often even more aggressive than other Trolls and given the right direction they can make effective shock troops for armies of Chaos. 

## **Bile Trolls**
According to the stories told by the vitki of the Kul, a warband of Trolls once wandered into the northern wastes to pit their might against the followers of the Dark Gods. They were led by Raak Stoneshatterer, a Troll of unusual drive, who sought in his hubris to win the attention of the Dark Gods by pitching his might aginst those of their chosen champions. 

On a plain of scorched bones, they won many victories but their fortunes changed when they faced the horde of Gulvas Bloatchild, a devotee of Nurgle. The Trolls struggled for days of bitter fighting but emerged victorious, and devoured the corpses of their foes. Their bodies were wracked by disease in doing so. The regenerative power of the Trolls struggled to heal the weeping sores that broke out upon their flesh and the cankers that ravaged their innards. They became twisted and tormented creatures, bloated and agonised, whose twisted bodies harboured all manner of infection. 

These days, descendants of the Trolls that once followed Raak can be found haunting the cold mires of Norsca and the Troll Country. These Bile Trolls are shunned and feared, even by other Trolls, who fear their tainted curse. 

## Olde Weirde’s Incunabulum
I have published a number of papers over the years that have touched on the subject of Trolls. I pride myself in some knowledge of the creatures and have been in correspondence with experts on the subject. However, criticism has come my way for never actually coming face to face with the creatures, and therefore my works condemned as bookish and impractical. I admit that there is some truth to this, but that is because there is danger inherent in the study of such creatures, and I offer the following anecdote. I have not examined a decent specimen since, for reasons that should become apparent. The truth is that there can be no Troll specimens suitable for study except those which are burned almost beyond usefulness. 

We were in the Teufel valley, having had an eventful journey back from Parravon by means of the Grey Lady Pass. The couple of weeks we had spent at the Duke of Parravon’s pleasure had delayed us long enough that we were traversing the pass just as the famous Grey Mountain winter was taking hold. This, in turn, had made our daily travel harder, and we were having to push on to make up for lost time. So that is why we were left in the valley as night fell and still a couple of miles short of our anticipated wayside inn. 

For several minutes, we could hear a strange keening noise that kept pace with us, as if it were following, or rather hunting, us. Then from out of the snowy woodlands, the sinuous, hulking creature emerged. It swung a tree trunk at von Gronighof, who was only saved as Kaia pushed him out of its way, and Sovrissniz fired two shots at the creature’s belly. I was pleased she had the wherewithal to keep her pistols loaded, even in these inhospitable conditions. 

Then Kaia stepped up and slashed at the Troll with her thin Elven blade and Sovrissniz drew her axe.  Eventually, and with at least a dozen wounds upon its body, the Troll collapsed. Later that evening, Professor Pfaff said that he had joined the fight and managed to get a telling blow on the creature with his hammer, and I do not necessarily dispute this. 

We had a huge Troll carcass on our hands, and were not too far from the inn, so we slung the thing on our cart. It would be remiss of us, as scientists, offered this opportunity to examine such a creature, that our intellectual curiosity did not trump our desire to get to warmth and safety. And in a few hours, we had the thing in the stables at the Monk’s Head Inn. 

The first thing to do was to discern the precise type of Troll it was. According to Ignatius of Nuln, with whom I have since had the pleasure of not inconsiderable correspondence, there are twenty-three main varieties of Troll, but at the time I was only aware of three, the common Troll, the river or marsh Troll, and the stone or mountain Troll. 

The Common Troll is not well named, as although it may be the most commonly encountered within the bounds of the Empire, this is by no means a common occurrence, thank Sigmar. Von Gronighof once shared a childhood experience where he had witnessed one from afar, happily pulling the legs off a deer. They are large, brutish creatures and any tool more complicated than a club is beyond their faculties. Yet, they have proven cunning ambush predators, concealing themselves as best they can alongside roads to surprise unwary travellers. 

River Trolls are rarely found beyond the confines of their native marshland. They make their homes only in the most stagnant and fetid waters where their green hides and pondweed-like hair makes them easily mistakable for floating detritus. Their stench is said to be the worst of all their kind. Having smelt the specimen under discussion here, I am in no rush to make the comparison. Reports that their vast and bloated matriarchs possess the capacity to wield magic is something no scholar should take at face value. 

The third variant is the Stone Troll. Sovrissniz considers herself an expert on these, and after a few Bugman’s will expound at length. They live in mountainous, rocky terrain, and are not above eating the rocks themselves to fill their bellies when there is not enough meat. And so their hides have taken on something of this nature, making their skin rock hard and helping them blend in with the terrain. Given that Dwarfs also favour such places, it is no surprise Sovrissniz has such a dislike for the creatures. 

As we were in the mountains, but also by a river, and as the creatures are decidedly uncommon, we could not narrow it down. Pfaff opined that by the creature’s rough, armoured hide and our journey through the mountains, it must be a Stone Troll, surmising that it may have followed us down from the high pass. Von Gronighof suggested that as it had ambushed us at the riverbank, it must therefore be a River Troll. I suggested that because we had encountered it at all, on the balance of probability it must be a Common Troll. 

We decided that a vivisection might shed some light on the issue, and after herding the horses to one end of the stable and borrowing a dozen lanterns from the landlady, we were able to create an adequate theatre for the examination. 

Von Gronighof decided to examine the stomach contents first, but as we turned it onto its back, we noticed several eyes in its stomach. One of the eyes flickered open and seemed to look at us, coldly and blankly. Pfaff said a quick prayer to Sigmar for protection, for we all instantly knew that there was the influence of the Dark Gods, here. 

Thinking back on the incident, I believe a question remains unanswered, one that no amount of slicing with von Gronighof’s knife could uncover. Was this a creature intrinsic to the Dark Gods, like the Beastmen of the forest, or was this a conventional, for want of a better word, Troll that had been touched and mutated by the dark gods, much like a forsaken Human can be? 

And so von Gronighof pierced the creature and dragged his knife across its belly. I am not able to adequately describe the contents of that foul creature’s stomach as they spilled across the floor. I feel safe to say this was the most foul substance I have ever come across. It was black and green and viscous and bubbling and acrid. Despite the airy stables, and the straw we had strewn across the ground, the corrosive stench of the stuff immediately made me heave and my own gastric fluids spilled to the floor in sympathy. 

It took me several minutes to recover, and in the interests of science, I was eventually able to force myself to view the scene. I could see bits of recognisable objects among the bile and can recall what looked like the melted remains of a two-handed sword, the broken skull of a mountain goat, half a wagon wheel, part of a stone statue of Sigmar, which annoyed Pfaff, most of a four-person tent, part of a stuffed bear, and a bowl for melted cheese. 

These objects were all in a state of barely recognisable decay, pitted and worn away by the strong stomach fluids of the Troll. A curious detail I have heard is that in battle, a beleaguered Troll is able to vomit up such juices as a means of attack, and I now understand why that would make such a fearful weapon. The very stones of the stable floor began to smoke and dissolve where the vomit had splashed upon them. 

The fumes were enough to have me wiping tears from my stinging eyes and my nose began to run profusely. I was not able to continue the autopsy for much longer, and I retired to the bar. Kaia and Professor Pfaff soon joined me. When I had fully recovered, I was able to force down quite a satisfying meal to replace the one I had left on the stable floor. 

Von Gronighof, however, was looking extremely green when I left him. I think it was due to a matter of professional pride that he continued the examination in the face of such unpleasant viscera. And Sovrissniz, I think, was unable to admit that she was daunted by the prospect of a creature’s stomach contents, so she stayed by the professor’s side throughout, just to prove that she could. 

It turned out to be extremely fortunate that she did, for when the creature awoke, disturbed by von Gronighof’s fiddling around inside its stomach, no doubt, it grabbed the professor and threw him across the stable. The professor hit his head on the corner of a manger and lost consciousness. 

Sovrissniz was quick enough, and bright enough, to grab her hammer and smash the many lamps we had hung around the place, showering the musty straw of the stable with flaming oil. In a few moments the stable was violently ablaze and so was the Troll. Once the alarm was raised, we all ran to help and the horses were rescued, and Sovrissniz managed to drag von Gronighof to safety. So there was no real harm done, except we had to pay for a new stable. 

And that is how we learned why there can be no safe practical study of Trolls. They must be burned (or, I have heard, pickled, or immersed in brandy, or honey, or acid) to prevent them from recovering from their injuries and springing back to life again, as if they had never been wounded in the first place. This does inhibit the study of the anatomy of Trolls, for there is only so much one can glean from blackened flesh. 

But perhaps the greatest lesson we could have learned is the extent of their ability to do such a thing, and why we should never attempt an examination of a fresh Troll corpse in the future. And von Gronighof still has the scars to remind him of the wisdom of this. 

## **Templates for Trolls**
Trolls do not possess much in the way of personality and are incapable of complex learning. As such, Trolls do not typically use the templates as Orcs, Goblins, and Ogres do. However, Trolls do adapt depending on their circumstances. The environment within which they live and their diets and experiences can lead them to develop distinct traits and attributes. 

In order to create a unique Troll, a GM must first decide what type it is. There are Type Templates for four types of Troll, and only one of these templates can be applied. 

## **River Troll Type Template**
River Trolls lurk in stagnant swamps and overgrown river banks. To their rank body odour is added the fetid stink of a river bottom. The reeking stench is enough to overcome the hardiest constitutions.

- River Troll 

Chaos Trolls are larger and more vicious than other types of Troll, and always bear signs of mutation. 

- Chaos Troll 

- Bile Troll 

There are then four types of Character Template that can be applied to a Troll. These can either be applied singly, or in combination. A Troll may therefore end up with 5 templates applied, provided it meets the required criteria. 

- Old Troll 

- Hungry Troll 

- Hulking Troll 

- Troll Hag (may only apply if the River Troll Template has been applied first)

Stone Trolls live in mountainous areas. In times of privation, they eat the stone itself and have absorbed its qualities. They have tough, rock-like hides and display a degree of resistance to magic.

## **River Troll Hag Template**
Giant River Troll Hags are hateful and bitter creatures, far larger and more dangerous than their common kin and able to shape the Winds of Magic. They prey upon anything foolish to enter the brackish waters in which they dwell and are often used as warnings to teach children not to wander into swamps or close to riverbanks. Troll Hags savour the flesh of Human children over that of any other creature. 

The sight of a Giant River Troll Hag shambling from the water in pursuit of her prey is truly terrifying. Her massive bulk glistens with stinking swamp slime as she hefts a huge, crudely wrought net stuffed with entrapped food. Like other Trolls, Troll Hags have a voracious appetite and will eat anything. All manner of things can be found in their nets, including writhing bog-octopi, recently captured soldiers, gleaming treasures hauled from the deeps, and other fermented morsels. 

Orcs sometimes lure Troll Hags from their lairs, using live Goblins on the ends of long fishing lines as bait to draw them forth. With their bellies full, the Troll Hag can be convinced to join an Orc horde onto the field of battle, their fearsome nature, massive strength, and their ability to cast hexes and curses upon their foes making them terrible enemies indeed.

## **Tactics**
Trolls are not strategically minded, being more like wild beasts in their attitudes and understanding of the world around them. They can employ simple strategies in order to better capture prey, but their repertoire of tricks is limited and simple. 

**Use of the Environment.** Trolls can set up an ambush near treacherous or confined environmental hazards. Tight mountain passes, sucking quagmires, tunnels, and icy crevasses are favoured locations. The Trolls wait until their intended victims are already struggling to navigate the hazard when they appear from their hiding places to launch an attack. If the habitat is already host to another monster, such as a lurking Bog Octopus in a swamp or a Manticore in a mountain cave, then so much the better. The Trolls will pick on the survivors of such an encounter, or feast on the fallen should there be any remains. 

**Pack Hunting.** Trolls often hunt in packs of three. It isn’t known why this number is so typical of groups of Trolls, but larger groups tend to fall into infighting or result in the larger Trolls stealing all the best food for themselves and leaving the smaller Trolls to starve. A Troll pack often splits into two groups. One Troll will make itself visible to prospective prey, either distracting them or casuing them to manoeuvre in order to avoid it. This Troll may appear within sight of a defensible position, such as a rocky outcrop or ruined building. The prospective prey may seek shelter, but then find themselves confronted by the other two Trolls. 

**Simple Traps.** Trolls are not good at engineering traps, but some crude construction has been attributed to them. A trick employed by some Stone Trolls is to line a steep mountain track with loose boulders. Those clambering over may cause a rockslide. River Trolls may use logs, clumps of bogweed, and matted rushes to create an apparently dry causeway through a bog, which becomes treacherous after a short distance. 

## **Presents!**
## **Easy Encounter**
The Goblins of the Crooked Maw Tribe are known to harass travellers along the passes of the Grey Mountains. These Goblins have devised a cunning method by which they can lure Trolls to fight with them without becoming a snack themselves. One method is to trick travellers into following them to a Troll’s lair, where Goblins can present them as a tasty treat. A Troll with a full belly is rather more pliable than a peckish individual. 

This encounter should be challenging for a new group, as they have to deal with both the Goblins and the Troll. Once they have attracted the attention of the travellers, they will be focused on self-preservation and staying out of reach until the Troll has dealt with their intended victims. 

For its part, the Troll will attack anyone, including any careless Goblins that stray too close. It will tend to prioritise whatever individual is makign the most noise, or dressed in the most colourful clothing. A fully armoured knight or brightly uniformed wizard will likely attract their attention. 

This encounter consists of: 

- An Old Stone Troll appears in the second Round. 

- Three Goblin Soldiers with spears and two Goblin Skirmishers with bows and arrows. 

- One spokes-Goblin, a Soldier with a sword and shield. This is not the leader, but the one pushed to the front to call the Troll out. 

**Bait.** Trolls have little use for precious artefacts such as gold, jewels, pieces of armour, and so on. In desperation, they may eat such items, but precious metals and jewels are hard to digest and make an unsatisfying meal. Trolls can learn to create trails of coins or gems in order to lure prospective prey into a vulnerable location. 

## **The Rocky Road Medium Encounter**
Trios of Stone Trolls gather near high-walled crevasses, where travellers are vulnerable. They emerge from their hiding places, hurling boulders or other debris, before charging in to snatch the best prizes. Whether they are working together or competing for the same food source may be debatable, but whilst living enemies are within reach, they will cooperate to slay them. 

The one main advantage defenders have is that the Trolls are too dim-witted to vary their approach. Should anyone survive to tell of the attacks, travellers can plan accordingly. Still, it is very difficult to spy a Stone Troll in hiding in rocky terrain, even if you know they are there. 

Before the encounter begins, Characters should make an **Opposed Perception/Stealth** Test, as the Trolls lie very still and are well camouflaged before they attack. The Trolls will be split up, so that one Troll attacks the Characters from the front, one from the left, and one to the right. 

The Trolls commence their attack by hurling boulders towards the rear of the party. This is done more to block the route of escape than it is to kill opponents, but if a Troll should strike an opponent with a boulder despite its poor BS, the effect would be comparable to that of being struck by a Rock Lobber (see pages 40 and 41). 

The Trolls will attack until they have rendered at least one of their targets _Prone_ or _Unconscious_ . At this point, they will try to abscond with their victim to devour it and will only fight to defend themselves. The Stone Trolls are as fond of mule meat as they are of Dwarfs and Humans, so allowing them to make off with a mount or draught animal may be a good way to escape from the clutches of the ravenous creatures. 

## **Heralds of the Horde Hard Encounter**
When the armies of Chaos march, they pass through the Troll Country where the largest Troll populations can be found. These creatures, often twisted by Chaos themselves, are often subsumed into the horde. Others are driven from their homelands, pushed ahead of the armies as the land’s resources are consumed. Such Troll migrations are among the first warnings of a Chaos incursion. 

A Heralds of the Horde encounter may well be extremely challenging. However, these warbands are hard to ignore and so they should have little difficulty persuading people of the threat. The Trolls will also have abandoned their ambush practices in favour of headlong assaults, desperately attacking and eating anything in their path. They are unlikely to give up the attack until either their victims or they themselves are dead. 

A Rocky Road encounter consists of: 

- Three Hungry Stone Trolls, attacking individually from the front and the sides. 

- A Hulking Chaos Troll and a Chaos Troll, forming the vanguard. 

- A Bile Troll, behind the front two. The other Trolls avoid the Bile Troll, and retreat from it if it comes too close. 

- An Old Chaos Troll (roll for an additional Mutation), half-a-mile behind the others. 

## **Cragtooth – Old Stone Troll**
Cragtooth is an ancient Troll. He lives in the mountains around Zhufbar and his litany of crimes takes up an entire page in the hold’s Book of Grudges. It is said the vicious Stone Troll even marched with the Goblins during the fall of Karak Varn, a legacy no Dwarf will soon forget. 

While sleeping in the weak sunlight, Cragtooth heard a strange whirring sound. He cracked an eye open and spied something like a bird, its wings spinning about its head. Fascinated, the Troll followed. The bird landed on a stone platform, carefully cut into the mountainside and, to Cragtooth’s astonishment, a Dwarf hopped out and began shovelling coal into her mount’s side. Cragtooth promptly ate the Dwarf, along with the gyrocopter. 

This began Cragtooth’s obsession with the flying machines. He watches the skies each day, waiting for the contraptions to pass. Of these, there is no shortage. The tunnels beneath Zhufbar are infested with Skaven. 

The Dwarfs need gyrocopters to communicate. Refuelling stations litter the mountains, kept stocked up by Zhufbar’s Rangers. Cragtooth takes great joy in finding them and devouring everything. 

For the first time in decades, the Dwarfs of Zhufbar have opened their Book of Grudges and begun writing new entries under Cragtooth’s name. The local Goblins, for their part, are happy to see Cragtooth up and about again and are already plotting how best to use his new taste for the Dwarfs’ machines to their advantage.

## **Grua Gribbleback - River Troll Hag**
High up in the Grey Mountains, the residents of Bögensee are isolated from the rest of the Reikland, close to the eerie ruins of Castle Drachenfels and the haunted stretches of the Grey Lady Pass. Sorrow and death are constant companions to those that live there. 

Recently, a great River Troll Hag named Grua Gribbleback has taken up residence downstream from the town, and is the latest in a line of monsters to bring tragedy to Bögensee’s inhabitants. As well as snatching the occasional hunter or trader for food, she is engaged in an eldritch ritual, the aim of which only she understands. 

Every day, she weaves body parts, pond slime, and river weeds into a strange cat’s cradle, which she stretches across the bed of the River Bögen, close to its source by the lake of Bögensee. What she hopes to achieve is a mystery, but the winds of magic are slowing through the area, stagnating into _Dhar_ . The effects are subtle, so far. There are perhaps a few more accidents, a few more deaths, more mutation and disease. But Grua’s net grows each day, and with it the festering dark magic.
